name: Verdure
lede: Verdure is an old word for the greenness of growing plants, and the swatch is a deep, shaded forest green.

sections.title: The greenness of plants
sections.body:
A dictionary of colour defines verdure as greenness of vegetation, or the color of vegetation, with *verdurous* meaning rich in green [1]. It belongs with French *verdeur* and *vert*, which descend from Latin *viridis* [2].

The word has always carried praise. A medieval writer quoted by Pastoureau calls the verdure of blossoming fields and leafy trees the most pleasant thing in the world [3]. He separates that pure natural green from the less noble green of dyers and painters [3]. Jean Robertet's poem, in the same book, has Green speak as a color that delights in perfect verdure and belongs only to joyful people [2]. Birren uses the word plainly, for the overhanging plant cover that a turtle is said to avoid [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch is a dark blue-green. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 31 hold it as a large enough patch (0.13 per cent), as photographed [5]. Most of its weight sits in shadows, 55 per cent against 13 per cent in highlights [5]. It is rare overall but strongly tied to one painter: Paul Gauguin has it in 3 of his 50 paintings here, about 46 times the archive's rate, and Post-Impressionism as a movement shows it about 34 times more often than average [5]. Aged varnish darkens greens, so part of that depth is the photograph.
